items.readable_text:
Content:
A curve or function is defined parametrically if [MATH: x] and [MATH: y] are given in terms of a third parameter [MATH: t.] This can often give rise to some interesting shapes.

Content:
For example, we can define a curve as
[MATH: x=t^3-3t, \qquad y=3t^2-9, \qquad -\infty < t <\infty.]
If we plot the curve, it looks as follows:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/9a71e8e1c9acee60bd6aed4e0946f6ca]

Content:
If we're given a parametric curve, how do we calculate [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}?] The answer is to use the chain rule.

Content:
The chain rule states that
[MATH: \frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t} \cdot \frac{\mathrm{d}t}{\mathrm{d}x}.]

Content:
We can rearrange this formula into a nicer version, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: (dy)/(dx)|= (dy)/(dt) ⋅ (dt)/(dx); = (dy)/(dt) ⋅ (1)/(dx/dt); = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt); = (y^{′}(t))/(x^{′}(t))]

Content:
Let's use the above formula to calculate [MATH: \dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}] for the given parametric curve
[MATH: x=t^3-3t, \qquad y=3t^2-9.]
Differentiating [MATH: x] and [MATH: y,] we get
[MATH: x'(t)=3t^2-3, \qquad y'(t)=6t.]
Therefore, we have
[MATH: (dy)/(dx)|= (y^{′}(t))/(x^{′}(t)); = (6t)/(3t^{2} − 3); = (2t)/(t^{2} − 1).]

Content:
Since the curve is defined in terms of the parameter [MATH: t,] the derivative is also defined in terms of [MATH: t.]

For the parametric curve
[MATH: x=\cos{t}, \quad y=\sin{t}, \qquad 0\leq t<2\pi,] calculate [MATH: \dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}.]

[IMG: /graphics/0f8bfc82b98e63e586e9d2e96d1acc5d]

sections.normalized_html:
We will use the formula [MATH: \frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{y'(t)}{x'(t)}.]

Differentiating [MATH: x] and [MATH: y,] we get

[MATH: x'(t) = -\sin{t}, \qquad y'(t)=\cos{t}.]

Therefore, [MATH: \frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{\cos t}{-\sin t} = -\cot t.]

items.title: Calculating the Slope of the Tangent to a Parametric Curve at a Given Point

sections.normalized_html: For the parametric curve [MATH: x=te^t, \quad y=e^{-t}, \qquad -\infty < t <\infty,] calculate the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point where [MATH: t=1.]
sections.readable_text:
For the parametric curve
[MATH: x=te^t, \quad y=e^{-t}, \qquad -\infty < t <\infty,]
calculate the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point where [MATH: t=1.]

sections.normalized_html:
We will use the formula [MATH: \frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{y'(t)}{x'(t)}.]

Differentiating [MATH: x] and [MATH: y,] we get

[MATH: x'(t) = e^t + te^t = (1+t)e^t, \qquad y'(t)=-e^{-t}.]

So we have [MATH: (dy)/(dx)|= (− e^{− t})/((1 + t)e^{t}); = − (1)/((1 + t)e^{2t}).]

Therefore, when [MATH: t=1,] the slope of the tangent to the curve is [MATH: (dy)/(dx)|_{t = 1}|= − (1)/(e^{2(1)}(1 + 1)); = − (1)/(2e^{2}).]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
A curve or function is defined parametrically if [MATH: x] and [MATH: y] are given in terms of a third parameter [MATH: t.] This can often give rise to some interesting shapes.

Content:
For example, we can define a curve as
[MATH: x=t^3-3t, \qquad y=3t^2-9, \qquad -\infty < t <\infty.]
If we plot the curve, it looks as follows:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/9a71e8e1c9acee60bd6aed4e0946f6ca]

Content:
If we're given a parametric curve, how do we calculate [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}?] The answer is to use the chain rule.

Content:
The chain rule states that
[MATH: \frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t} \cdot \frac{\mathrm{d}t}{\mathrm{d}x}.]

Content:
We can rearrange this formula into a nicer version, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: (dy)/(dx)|= (dy)/(dt) ⋅ (dt)/(dx); = (dy)/(dt) ⋅ (1)/(dx/dt); = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt); = (y^{′}(t))/(x^{′}(t))]

Content:
Let's use the above formula to calculate [MATH: \dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}] for the given parametric curve
[MATH: x=t^3-3t, \qquad y=3t^2-9.]
Differentiating [MATH: x] and [MATH: y,] we get
[MATH: x'(t)=3t^2-3, \qquad y'(t)=6t.]
Therefore, we have
[MATH: (dy)/(dx)|= (y^{′}(t))/(x^{′}(t)); = (6t)/(3t^{2} − 3); = (2t)/(t^{2} − 1).]

Content:
Since the curve is defined in terms of the parameter [MATH: t,] the derivative is also defined in terms of [MATH: t.]

---

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We will use the formula
[MATH: \frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{y'(t)}{x'(t)}.]

Differentiating [MATH: x] and [MATH: y,] we get

[MATH: x'(t) = -\sin{t}, \qquad y'(t)=\cos{t}.]

Therefore,
[MATH: \frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{\cos t}{-\sin t} = -\cot t.]

Item 5 — Example: Calculating the Slope of the Tangent to a Parametric Curve at a Given Point

Example Prompt:
For the parametric curve
[MATH: x=te^t, \quad y=e^{-t}, \qquad -\infty < t <\infty,]
calculate the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point where [MATH: t=1.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We will use the formula
[MATH: \frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{y'(t)}{x'(t)}.]

Differentiating [MATH: x] and [MATH: y,] we get

[MATH: x'(t) = e^t + te^t = (1+t)e^t, \qquad y'(t)=-e^{-t}.]

So we have
[MATH: (dy)/(dx)|= (− e^{− t})/((1 + t)e^{t}); = − (1)/((1 + t)e^{2t}).]

Therefore, when [MATH: t=1,] the slope of the tangent to the curve is
[MATH: (dy)/(dx)|_{t = 1}|= − (1)/(e^{2(1)}(1 + 1)); = − (1)/(2e^{2}).]
